summary: Initial discovery for Dedicated capacity. Oxbridge is evaluating reserved GPU pools for low-latency customer-facing LLM features. Key concerns: data isolation, burst capacity, scaling policies, SSO/KMS integrations, and cost tradeoffs. Agreed to run benchmarks and share pricing + compliance docs.
topics: Reserved capacity sizing and burst strategy
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Carlos, our solution engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Laura Chen: Hi Maya, hey Carlos. Good, thanks.
[00:10] Samir Patel: Afternoon.
[00:11] Marcus Bell: Yep, all good.
[00:13] Maya Patel: Awesome. The goal today is a dedicated capacity discovery — we want to understand your latency targets, isolation needs, burst patterns, and how you expect to scale. We'll also cover security and next steps. Laura, do you want to kick off with your use case?
[00:27] Laura Chen: Sure. So at Oxbridge we're rolling out a generative assistant across our customer portal — mortgage and wealth management workflows. It's customer-facing so latency and PII handling are big. We're currently prototyping on hosted endpoints like OpenAI for dev, but for prod we need reserved capacity for predictable SLOs and stricter isolation.
[00:45] Carlos Ruiz: Got it. When you say predictable SLOs, what are you targeting for p95 latency and concurrency?
[00:52] Laura Chen: Ideally p95 under 400ms for short completions (<=256 tokens) and p95 under 800ms for longer sessions. Concurrency is tricky — our peak is roughly 150 concurrent interactive sessions during day, with higher token rates during statement generation overnight.
[01:09] Samir Patel: To add, we have spikes when statement batches run — those are heavy token generation but can be scheduled. We need burst capability though because sometimes business events cause sudden traffic.
[01:19] Maya Patel: Thanks. That's useful. Carlos, from a Dedicated perspective, we typically size reserved GPU pools based on steady-state baseline and allow burst capacity via shared spare nodes or burst credits to handle spikes. We also support autoscaling policies with warm pools to keep latency low.
[01:35] Carlos Ruiz: Yeah, the main knob is how many reserved GPUs vs how much burst you want. For Oxbridge's numbers, a starting config might be a small reserved pool sized for your daytime peak and then policy for burst to our shared host or pre-warmed nodes. Do you have any constraints around mixed tenancy?
[01:51] Laura Chen: No mixed tenancy — we need single-tenant GPUs. Data residency and isolation are musts. So Dedicated with private VPC and customer-managed keys would be preferable.
[02:01] Marcus Bell: On keys, we use an on-prem KMS for critical keys. We need to understand whether Redwood integrates with external HSM/KMS or if keys are stored in cloud KMS only.
[02:10] Carlos Ruiz: We support external KMS integrations and bring-your-own-key patterns; we've done HSM integrations with customers in finance. We'll include details in the security pack.
[02:18] Jill Thompson: From procurement, we also need to see SLA language and uplift pricing for guaranteed capacity.
[02:24] Maya Patel: Absolutely. We'll send the Dedicated pricing deck and the SLA summary.
[02:28] Samir Patel: Can you talk about version pinning and rollouts? We want to be able to pin a model version for compliance and roll forward with canaries.
[02:36] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, Dedicated supports model version pinning, canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a smaller model family if a node fails or there's capacity issues. You can define routing policies — latency-first, cost-first, region-priority.
[02:50] Laura Chen: About fallback — we can't degrade to an external hosted provider because of data residency. Does the fallback always stay within your customer's Dedicated footprint?
[02:59] Carlos Ruiz: Good question. Fallback stays to compatible model variants within the customer's Dedicated or Private deployments. We only route externally if the customer has explicitly allowed cross-tenant fallbacks, which it sounds like you won't.
[03:12] Maya Patel: Can we dig into burst behavior? You mentioned warm pools — how quickly can you spin up capacity and what are cold start implications?
[03:20] Carlos Ruiz: Warm pools are pre-initialized containers with model weights loaded; they can accept requests in tens to low hundreds of milliseconds for short sequences. Cold starts (loading model weights onto GPU) can take several minutes for large models, so the warm pool approach helps maintain p95 latency during burst. For heavy batch jobs, we recommend scheduled capacity.
[03:36] Samir Patel: We also will run nightly statement generation which is high throughput. Can we use separate reserved clusters for batch vs interactive to avoid contention?
[03:44] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, many customers separate interactive and batch workloads onto different pools; routing policies and autoscaling can be tuned per-route. That prevents batch jobs from impacting customer-facing latency.
[03:52] Laura Chen: What's your quantization support? We want a mix of accuracy and cost-savings.
[03:58] Carlos Ruiz: We support INT8 and mixed quantization for many open models; our runtime picks optimized kernels and we test quality regressions as part of the onboarding. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per workload. We'll run a quality baseline during the POC.
[04:13] Marcus Bell: Networking specifics — we need egress controls and we can't have outbound calls to third-party telemetry services. Is that configurable?
[04:20] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, Dedicated in a VPC supports strict egress controls, and telemetry endpoints can be configured to your endpoints only.
[04:27] Jill Thompson: On security docs, can you share SOC 2 and penetration testing summaries?
[04:31] Maya Patel: We'll include SOC 2, ISO summaries, pen test reports, and our audit log docs in the packet.
[04:37] Laura Chen: For benchmarking, we'd like to replicate our prompt set. What's the best way to hand that over?
[04:42] Carlos Ruiz: Send us a representative prompt set and traffic profile — number of calls per minute, tokens per call distribution, and sample prompts. Carlos to provide runbook for benchmark runs.
[04:50] Samir Patel: What's pricing like for reserved GPUs vs hosted per-token?
[04:55] Maya Patel: Reserved capacity is priced as a monthly commit per GPU type with included throughput and lower per-token rates. We usually show a TCO spreadsheet comparing your expected token volume on Hosted vs Dedicated. We'll share a model with scenarios for starter, steady-state, and heavy-burst.
[05:09] Laura Chen: Any limits on model catalog for Dedicated? We plan to use an open Llama variant and also evaluate some proprietary models.
[05:17] Carlos Ruiz: You can bring open models; we also support curated model catalog. Proprietary models can be deployed into Dedicated if you provide the weights and license allows serving. There's a model onboarding checklist we will send.
[05:28] Marcus Bell: For observability, do you give per-token cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards?
[05:33] Maya Patel: Yes, Redwood Console includes token-level cost breakdowns, per-route latency, tracing hooks and error analysis; logs can be sent to your S3 or SIEM depending on retention.
[05:43] Laura Chen: What's the onboarding timeline for Dedicated? We have a regulatory review, so earliest pilot would be in 6–8 weeks.
[05:51] Maya Patel: Typical Dedicated onboarding is 4–8 weeks depending on model complexity and compliance reviews — 6–8 weeks for you seems reasonable.
[05:58] Samir Patel: If we start a POC, will you do a benchmark on our workload?
[06:02] Carlos Ruiz: Yes. We'll run a benchmark using your prompt set against a proposed Dedicated config and provide latency/cost breakdowns and recommended config (reserved GPUs, burst policy, quantization).
[06:11] Jill Thompson: Procurement will need contract terms and data processing addendums.
[06:15] Maya Patel: We'll include our standard DPA and enterprise contract templates for review.
[06:19] Laura Chen: A couple of technical follow-ups — how does KV cache persist across sessions and does it respect tenant boundaries?
[06:26] Carlos Ruiz: KV cache is per-model-instance and tenant-aware. We isolate caches for Dedicated customers; long-lived context can be cached to reduce tokens and latency. We also provide cache invalidation hooks.
[06:36] Samir Patel: Any recommendations for burst sizing? How many warm nodes should we keep for a 150 concurrency p95 400ms target?
[06:44] Carlos Ruiz: Rough back-of-envelope: depends on model and token rates, but starting with a warm pool sized at 30–40% of your expected peak concurrency helps. We'll run benchmarks to refine — that's why the POC is useful.
[06:58] Laura Chen: Typo: benchamrks -> benchmarks.
[07:01] (laughter)
[07:04] Marcus Bell: One last question on audit logs — retention and immutability options?
[07:10] Maya Patel: We can push logs to your S3 with lifecycle rules; immutable retention can be set in your storage backend. We'll document retention options.
[07:18] Maya Patel: Alright, wrapping up. Recap: Maya sends pricing + SLA and contract templates; Carlos sends benchmark runbook and quantization notes; Oxbridge provides prompt set, traffic profile, and compliance contacts. We'll schedule a POC scoping call for mid-March. Any other items?
[07:36] Laura Chen: No, that's it from me. Thanks.
[07:38] Samir Patel: Thanks everyone.
[07:39] Marcus Bell: Thanks.
[07:40] Maya Patel: Great, talk soon.
[07:42] [END]
